claim: mTOR in CD4 T cells is essential for Tfh differentiation.
source: We report here that mTOR in CD4 T cells is essential for Tfh differentiation.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript showing impaired Tfh differentiation in mTOR-deficient mice.

claim: In Mtorf/f-Cd4Cre mice, both constitutive and inducible Tfh differentiation is severely impaired.
source: In Mtorf/f-Cd4Cre mice, both constitutive and inducible Tfh differentiation is severely impaired, leading to defective germinal center B cell formation and antibody production.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figures 1 and 4 showing reduced Tfh cell percentages and numbers in mTOR-deficient mice.

claim: mTOR deficiency in CD4 T cells leads to defective germinal center B cell formation.
source: In Mtorf/f-Cd4Cre mice, both constitutive and inducible Tfh differentiation is severely impaired, leading to defective germinal center B cell formation and antibody production.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figures 1 and 4 showing reduced GC B cell percentages and numbers.

claim: mTOR deficiency in CD4 T cells leads to defective antibody production.
source: In Mtorf/f-Cd4Cre mice, both constitutive and inducible Tfh differentiation is severely impaired, leading to defective germinal center B cell formation and antibody production.
evidence: Supported by ELISA data in Figures 1e and 4f showing reduced serum immunoglobulin levels.

claim: Both mTORC1 and mTORC2 contribute to Tfh and GC B cell development.
source: Moreover, both mTORC1 and mTORC2 contribute to Tfh and GC B cell development but may do so via distinct mechanisms.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments with Raptor-deficient and Rictor-deficient mice showing reduced Tfh and GC B cell responses in both genotypes.

claim: mTORC1 and mTORC2 contribute to Tfh differentiation via distinct mechanisms.
source: Moreover, both mTORC1 and mTORC2 contribute to Tfh and GC B cell development but may do so via distinct mechanisms.
evidence: Supported by data showing mTORC1 affects proliferation while mTORC2 affects Akt activation and TCF1 expression without grossly affecting proliferation.

claim: mTORC1 mainly promotes CD4 T cell proliferation to reach the cell divisions necessary for Tfh differentiation.
source: mTORC1 mainly promotes CD4 T cell proliferation to reach the cell divisions necessary for Tfh differentiation, while Rictor/mTORC2 regulates Tfh differentiation by promoting Akt activation and TCF1 expression without grossly influencing T cell proliferation.
evidence: Demonstrated by CFSE dilution experiments in Figure 7a showing impaired proliferation of Raptor-deficient OT2 T cells.

claim: Rictor/mTORC2 regulates Tfh differentiation by promoting Akt activation.
source: mTORC1 mainly promotes CD4 T cell proliferation to reach the cell divisions necessary for Tfh differentiation, while Rictor/mTORC2 regulates Tfh differentiation by promoting Akt activation and TCF1 expression without grossly influencing T cell proliferation.
evidence: Supported by Western blot and flow cytometry data in Figure 8a-b showing decreased Akt S473 phosphorylation in Rictor-deficient cells.

claim: Rictor/mTORC2 regulates Tfh differentiation by promoting TCF1 expression.
source: mTORC1 mainly promotes CD4 T cell proliferation to reach the cell divisions necessary for Tfh differentiation, while Rictor/mTORC2 regulates Tfh differentiation by promoting Akt activation and TCF1 expression without grossly influencing T cell proliferation.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 8f showing decreased TCF1 expression in Rictor-deficient Tfh cells.

claim: Rictor/mTORC2 does not grossly influence T cell proliferation.
source: mTORC1 mainly promotes CD4 T cell proliferation to reach the cell divisions necessary for Tfh differentiation, while Rictor/mTORC2 regulates Tfh differentiation by promoting Akt activation and TCF1 expression without grossly influencing T cell proliferation.
evidence: Supported by CFSE dilution data in Figure 7f showing similar proliferation of Rictor-deficient and WT OT2 T cells.

claim: Tfh cells play critical roles for germinal center responses and effective humoral immunity.
source: T follicular helper (Tfh) cells play critical roles for germinal center responses and effective humoral immunity.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in immunology, supported by multiple citations in the introduction.

claim: About one-third of PP CD4 T cells from Mtorf/f(WT) mice were CXCR5+PD-1+ Tfh cells.
source: About one-third of PP CD4 T cells from Mtorf/f(WT) mice were CXCR5+PD-1+ Tfh cells (Figure 1a and b)
evidence: Quantified from flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1a and 1b.

claim: About 10% to 25% B220+CD93-IgM-IgD- B cells were GL7+Fas+ GC B-cells in WT mice.
source: about 10% to 25% B220+CD93-IgM-IgD- B cells were GL7+Fas+ GC B-cells (Figure 1c and d).
evidence: Quantified from flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1c and 1d.

claim: Both percentages and absolute numbers of Tfh cells substantially decreased in mLNs and PPs from Mtorf/f-Cd4Cre mice compared with their littermate controls.
source: Both percentages (Figure 1a and b) and absolute numbers (right panel, Figure 1b) of Tfh cells substantially decreased in mLNs and PPs from Mtorf/f-Cd4Cre mice compared with their littermate controls.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data and quantification in Figure 1a and 1b.

claim: GC B-cell percentages and absolute numbers in Mtorf/f-Cd4Cre mLNs and PPs dramatically decreased.
source: Concordantly, GC B-cell percentages (Figure 1c and d) and absolute numbers (right panel, Figure 1d) in Mtorf/f-Cd4Cre mLNs and PPs also dramatically decreased
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data and quantification in Figure 1c and 1d.

claim: Decreased GC B cells in mTOR-deficient mice correlated with reduced serum IgG levels.
source: Concordantly, GC B-cell percentages (Figure 1c and d) and absolute numbers (right panel, Figure 1d) in Mtorf/f-Cd4Cre mLNs and PPs also dramatically decreased, correlated with reduced serum IgG but increased serum IgM levels (Figure 1e).
evidence: Demonstrated by ELISA data in Figure 1e showing reduced IgG levels in mTOR-deficient mice.

claim: Decreased GC B cells in mTOR-deficient mice correlated with increased serum IgM levels.
source: Concordantly, GC B-cell percentages (Figure 1c and d) and absolute numbers (right panel, Figure 1d) in Mtorf/f-Cd4Cre mLNs and PPs also dramatically decreased, correlated with reduced serum IgG but increased serum IgM levels (Figure 1e).
evidence: Demonstrated by ELISA data in Figure 1e showing increased IgM levels in mTOR-deficient mice.

claim: IgG1 and IgG2b but not IgG3 levels decreased in mTOR deficiency mice.
source: Interestingly, IgG1, and IgG2b but not IgG3 levels decreased in mTOR deficiency mice, suggesting that the IgG3 class-switch occurred independently of mTOR signaling in CD4 T cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by ELISA data in Figure 1e showing differential effects on IgG subclasses.

claim: IgG3 class-switch occurs independently of mTOR signaling in CD4 T cells.
source: Interestingly, IgG1, and IgG2b but not IgG3 levels decreased in mTOR deficiency mice, suggesting that the IgG3 class-switch occurred independently of mTOR signaling in CD4 T cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that IgG3 levels were not decreased in mTOR-deficient mice while other IgG subclasses were.

claim: IgA secreted in the intestinal lumen decreased in mTOR-deficient mice.
source: Additionally, IgA secreted in the intestinal lumen decreased (Figure 1e), which was consistent with impaired GC-responses in PPs.
evidence: Demonstrated by ELISA measurement of fecal IgA shown in Figure 1e.

claim: mTOR deficiency in T cells severely compromised constitutive Tfh and GC responses in PPs and mLNs.
source: Thus, mTOR deficiency in T cells severely compromised constitutive Tfh and GC responses in PPs and mLNs as well as overall humoral immunity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 1 showing reduced Tfh, GC B cells, and antibody levels.

claim: mTOR deficiency in T cells severely compromised overall humoral immunity.
source: Thus, mTOR deficiency in T cells severely compromised constitutive Tfh and GC responses in PPs and mLNs as well as overall humoral immunity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on reduced antibody production and GC responses shown in Figure 1.

claim: Both Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre and Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre mice contained fewer Tfh cells in mLNs and PPs compared to their respective controls.
source: Both Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre (Figure 2a,b) and Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre mice (Figure 2c,d) contained fewer Tfh cells in mLNs and PPs compared to their respective controls.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 2a-d showing reduced Tfh cells in both genotypes.

claim: GC B-cells decreased in mLNs and PPs in both Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre and Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre mice.
source: Coinciding with reduced Tfh cells, GC B-cells decreased in mLNs and PPs in both Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre (Figure 2e,f) and Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre mice (Figure 2g,h), although at magnitudes less severe than in Mtorf/f-Cd4Cre mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 2e-h showing reduced GC B cells in both genotypes.

claim: GC B-cell decreases in Raptor- and Rictor-deficient mice were at magnitudes less severe than in mTOR-deficient mice.
source: Coinciding with reduced Tfh cells, GC B-cells decreased in mLNs and PPs in both Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre (Figure 2e,f) and Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre mice (Figure 2g,h), although at magnitudes less severe than in Mtorf/f-Cd4Cre mice.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on the data from Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Total serum IgG but not IgM levels in Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre mice decreased compared with controls.
source: Moreover, total serum IgG but not IgM levels in Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre (Figure 2i) and Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre mice (Figure 2j) also decreased compared with controls.
evidence: Demonstrated by ELISA data in Figure 2i showing reduced IgG but not IgM in Raptor-deficient mice.

claim: Total serum IgG but not IgM levels in Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre mice decreased compared with controls.
source: Moreover, total serum IgG but not IgM levels in Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre (Figure 2i) and Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre mice (Figure 2j) also decreased compared with controls.
evidence: Demonstrated by ELISA data in Figure 2j showing reduced IgG but not IgM in Rictor-deficient mice.

claim: mTORC1 deficiency caused reduced IgG1 and IgG2b levels without obviously affecting IgG3.
source: Interestingly, mTORC1 deficiency caused reduced IgG1 and IgG2b levels without obviously affecting IgG3 (Figure 2i)
evidence: Demonstrated by ELISA data in Figure 2i showing differential effects on IgG subclasses in Raptor-deficient mice.

claim: mTORC2 deficiency resulted in decreases in IgG1, IgG2b, and IgG3 levels in serum.
source: while mTORC2 deficiency resulted in decreases in IgG1, IgG2b, and IgG3 levels in serum (Figure 2j).
evidence: Demonstrated by ELISA data in Figure 2j showing reduced levels of all three IgG subclasses in Rictor-deficient mice.

claim: Neither Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre nor Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre mice had reduced fecal IgA levels.
source: However, unlike mTOR-deficient mice, neither Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre nor Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre mice had reduced fecal IgA levels (Figure 2i,j).
evidence: Demonstrated by ELISA data in Figure 2i and 2j showing no significant reduction in fecal IgA.

claim: Both mTORC1 and mTORC2 contributed to constitutive Tfh and GC responses in mLNs and PPs.
source: Together, these observations suggested that both mTORC1 and mTORC2 contributed to constitutive Tfh and GC responses in mLNs and PPs and may synergistically or redundantly promote intestinal IgA responses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data from Figure 2 showing reduced Tfh and GC responses in both Raptor- and Rictor-deficient mice.

claim: mTORC1 and mTORC2 may synergistically or redundantly promote intestinal IgA responses.
source: Together, these observations suggested that both mTORC1 and mTORC2 contributed to constitutive Tfh and GC responses in mLNs and PPs and may synergistically or redundantly promote intestinal IgA responses.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that IgA was only reduced in mTOR-deficient mice but not in Raptor- or Rictor-deficient mice alone.

claim: CD4+Foxp3+ Treg percentages and Treg to Tcon ratios were similar to WT controls in the spleen, mLN, and PPs in Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre mice.
source: In Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre mice, CD4+Foxp3+ Treg percentages as well as Treg to Tcon ratios were similar to WT controls in the spleen, mLN, and PPs (Figure 3a–c).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 3a-c showing no significant differences in Treg percentages or ratios.

claim: Treg numbers in Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre mice were not obviously altered in the spleen and mLNs.
source: Treg numbers in Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre mice were not obviously altered in the spleen and mLNs, but they were decreased in the PPs compared with WT controls (Figure 3d).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 3d showing similar Treg numbers in spleen and mLNs.

claim: Treg numbers in Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre mice were decreased in the PPs compared with WT controls.
source: Treg numbers in Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre mice were not obviously altered in the spleen and mLNs, but they were decreased in the PPs compared with WT controls (Figure 3d).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 3d showing reduced Treg numbers in PPs.

claim: The decrease of total PP cell numbers was a major contributing factor for decreased PP Treg numbers in Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre mice.
source: The decrease of total PP cell numbers (14.17 ± 3.22 million in Rptorf/f vs 6.13 ± 0.72 million in Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre, p<0.05) was a major contributing factor for decreased PP Treg numbers in Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre mice.
evidence: This is stated explicitly with quantitative data comparing total PP cell numbers between genotypes.

claim: Treg percentages and numbers were decreased in the spleen and PPs in Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre mice.
source: In Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre mice, Treg percentages and numbers were decreased in the spleen and PPs, but they were not significantly decreased in mLNs (Figure 3g,h and j)
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 3g, h, and j showing reduced Treg percentages and numbers in spleen and PPs.

claim: Treg percentages and numbers were not significantly decreased in mLNs in Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre mice.
source: In Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre mice, Treg percentages and numbers were decreased in the spleen and PPs, but they were not significantly decreased in mLNs (Figure 3g,h and j)
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 3g, h, and j showing no significant reduction in mLN Tregs.

claim: Treg to Tcon ratios were not significantly skewed in Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre mice.
source: However, Treg to Tcon ratios were not significantly skewed (Figure 3i).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 3i showing similar Treg/Tcon ratios.

claim: The percentages of the Foxp3+ population within PP Tfh cells were decreased in Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre mice.
source: The percentages of the Foxp3+ population within PP Tfh cells were decreased and Foxp3+ Treg numbers were more severely decreased in Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre mice, suggesting that mTORC1 deficiency had a stronger effect on Tfr development/homeostasis than on conventional Tregs (Figure 3e,f).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 3e showing reduced Tfr percentages.

claim: Foxp3+ Treg numbers were more severely decreased in Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre mice.
source: The percentages of the Foxp3+ population within PP Tfh cells were decreased and Foxp3+ Treg numbers were more severely decreased in Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre mice, suggesting that mTORC1 deficiency had a stronger effect on Tfr development/homeostasis than on conventional Tregs (Figure 3e,f).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 3f showing reduced Tfr numbers.

claim: mTORC1 deficiency had a stronger effect on Tfr development/homeostasis than on conventional Tregs.
source: The percentages of the Foxp3+ population within PP Tfh cells were decreased and Foxp3+ Treg numbers were more severely decreased in Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre mice, suggesting that mTORC1 deficiency had a stronger effect on Tfr development/homeostasis than on conventional Tregs (Figure 3e,f).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Tfr were more severely affected than conventional Tregs in Raptor-deficient mice.

claim: PP Tfr percentages within Tfh cells were not decreased in Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre mice.
source: In Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre mice, PP Tfr percentages within Tfh cells were not decreased, but their numbers were decreased due to reduced Tfh numbers (Figure 3k,l).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 3k showing no significant reduction in Tfr percentages.

claim: PP Tfr numbers were decreased in Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre mice due to reduced Tfh numbers.
source: In Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre mice, PP Tfr percentages within Tfh cells were not decreased, but their numbers were decreased due to reduced Tfh numbers (Figure 3k,l).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 3l showing reduced Tfr numbers.

claim: Deficiency of either mTORC1 or mTORC2 did not increase the relative abundance of Tregs within CD4 T cells in the spleen, mLNs, and PPs.
source: Together, our data suggest that deficiency of either mTORC1 or mTORC2 did not increase the relative abundance of Tregs within CD4 T cells in the spleen, mLNs, and PPs or the Tfr ratios within Tregs in the PPs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the Treg data in Figure 3.

claim: Deficiency of either mTORC1 or mTORC2 did not increase the Tfr ratios within Tregs in the PPs.
source: Together, our data suggest that deficiency of either mTORC1 or mTORC2 did not increase the relative abundance of Tregs within CD4 T cells in the spleen, mLNs, and PPs or the Tfr ratios within Tregs in the PPs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the Tfr data in Figure 3.

claim: The decreased constitutive GC-B cell response was likely not caused by change of Treg or Tfr numbers in Rptor or Rictor deficient mice.
source: Together with decreased total Treg and Tfr numbers in Rptor or Rictor deficient PPs, these data suggest that the decreased constitutive GC-B cell response was likely not caused by change of Treg or Tfr numbers in these mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Treg and Tfr numbers were decreased rather than increased in the mutant mice.

claim: Fewer splenic Tfh cells were present in Mtorf/f-Cd4Cre mice than in WT controls 21 days after NP17-CGG immunization.
source: On day 21 after immunization, fewer splenic Tfh cells were present in Mtorf/f-Cd4Cre mice than in WT controls in both percentages and numbers (Figure 4a,b)
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 4a and 4b showing reduced Tfh cells after immunization.

claim: GC B-cells were concomitantly reduced in Mtorf/f-Cd4Cre mice 21 days after NP17-CGG immunization.
source: On day 21 after immunization, fewer splenic Tfh cells were present in Mtorf/f-Cd4Cre mice than in WT controls in both percentages and numbers (Figure 4a,b) with concomitantly reduced GC B-cells (Figure 4c,d).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 4c and 4d showing reduced GC B cells after immunization.

claim: Induction of Bcl-6 was blunted in splenic and mLN B cells from Mtorf/f-Cd4Cre mice after immunization.
source: Induction of Bcl-6, a transcription factor crucial for GC B cell differentiation (Fukuda et al., 1997), was blunted in splenic and mLN B cells from Mtorf/f-Cd4Cre mice after immunization (Figure 4e).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 4e showing reduced Bcl-6 expression in B cells.

claim: Bcl-6 is a transcription factor crucial for GC B cell differentiation.
source: Induction of Bcl-6, a transcription factor crucial for GC B cell differentiation (Fukuda et al., 1997), was blunted in splenic and mLN B cells from Mtorf/f-Cd4Cre mice after immunization (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Fukuda et al., 1997.

claim: Both total (NIP26) and high-affinity (NIP7) serum NIP-specific IgM and IgG levels were much lower in Mtorf/f-Cd4Cre mice than in WT mice 7, 14, and 21 days after immunization.
source: Moreover, both total (NIP26) and high-affinity (NIP7) serum NIP-specific IgM and IgG levels were much lower in Mtorf/f-Cd4Cre mice than in WT mice 7, 14, and 21 days after immunization (Figure 4f).
evidence: Demonstrated by ELISA data in Figure 4f showing reduced antigen-specific antibody responses.

claim: mTOR in CD4 T cells was essential for inducing Tfh differentiation following immunization.
source: Thus, mTOR in CD4 T cells was essential for inducing Tfh differentiation and GC B cell formation following immunization and for T-cell-dependent antigen-induced humoral immune responses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the immunization data in Figure 4.

claim: mTOR in CD4 T cells was essential for GC B cell formation following immunization.
source: Thus, mTOR in CD4 T cells was essential for inducing Tfh differentiation and GC B cell formation following immunization and for T-cell-dependent antigen-induced humoral immune responses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the immunization data in Figure 4.

claim: mTOR in CD4 T cells was essential for T-cell-dependent antigen-induced humoral immune responses.
source: Thus, mTOR in CD4 T cells was essential for inducing Tfh differentiation and GC B cell formation following immunization and for T-cell-dependent antigen-induced humoral immune responses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the immunization data in Figure 4.

claim: Both Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre and Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre mice contained fewer splenic Tfh cells than did WT controls after NP17-CGG immunization.
source: Both Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre (Figure 5a,b) and Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre mice (Figure 5c,d) contained fewer splenic Tfh cells than did WT controls
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 5a-d showing reduced Tfh cells in both genotypes after immunization.

claim: Decreased Tfh cells in Raptor- and Rictor-deficient mice correlated with decreased numbers of splenic GC B cells.
source: Both Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre (Figure 5a,b) and Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre mice (Figure 5c,d) contained fewer splenic Tfh cells than did WT controls, correlated with decreased numbers of splenic GC B cells in Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre (Figure 5e,f) and Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre (Figure 5g,h) mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 5e-h showing reduced GC B cells in both genotypes after immunization.

claim: NIP-specific total and high-affinity IgG and IgM antibody levels decreased in immunized Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre deficient mice.
source: Moreover, NIP-specific total and high-affinity IgG and IgM antibody levels decreased in immunized Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre deficient mice (Figure 5i), indicating impaired humoral immune responses.
evidence: Demonstrated by ELISA data in Figure 5i showing reduced antigen-specific antibody responses.

claim: Neither total nor high-affinity NIP-specific IgM levels decreased in Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre mice.
source: In comparison with Rptor-deficient mice, neither total nor high-affinity NIP-specific IgM levels decreased in Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre mice (Figure 5j).
evidence: Demonstrated by ELISA data in Figure 5j showing no significant reduction in IgM responses.

claim: Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre mice manifested a trend of mildly decreased NIP specific total and high-affinity IgG levels.
source: While Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre mice manifested a trend of mildly decreased NIP specific total and high-affinity IgG levels, only decreases of total IgG on day 7 and high-affinity IgG on day 14 were statistically significant (Figure 5j).
evidence: Demonstrated by ELISA data in Figure 5j showing mild reductions in IgG responses.

claim: GC numbers were obviously less in Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre spleens than in controls on day 14 after immunization.
source: As shown in Figure 5k,l, GC numbers were obviously less and sizes of individual GCs were noticeably smaller in Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre spleens than in controls
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy data in Figure 5k and 5l showing reduced GC numbers.

claim: Sizes of individual GCs were noticeably smaller in Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre spleens than in controls on day 14 after immunization.
source: As shown in Figure 5k,l, GC numbers were obviously less and sizes of individual GCs were noticeably smaller in Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre spleens than in controls
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy data in Figure 5k and 5l showing reduced GC sizes.

claim: Both mTORC1 and mTORC2 contributed to Tfh/GC B cell responses.
source: Together, both mTORC1 and mTORC2 contributed to Tfh/GC B cell responses, in which mTORC1 appeared to play a more important role than mTORC2.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the immunization data in Figure 5.

claim: mTORC1 appeared to play a more important role than mTORC2 in Tfh/GC B cell responses.
source: Together, both mTORC1 and mTORC2 contributed to Tfh/GC B cell responses, in which mTORC1 appeared to play a more important role than mTORC2.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that antibody responses were more severely affected in Raptor-deficient mice than in Rictor-deficient mice.

claim: Rptorf/f- or Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre OT2 T cells showed similar CD62L+CD44- naïve, CD62L+CD44+ CM, and CD62L-CD44+ EM ratios to those of their respective WT controls.
source: Rptorf/f- or Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre OT2 T cells showed similar CD62L+CD44- naïve, CD62L+CD44+ CM, and CD62L-CD44+ EM ratios to those of their respective WT controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a showing similar memory/naïve ratios.

claim: Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre naïve OT2 T cells expressed similar CD25, CD122, CD69, and CD44 but decreased CD127 (IL7Rα) compared to its WT control.
source: Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre naïve OT2 T cells expressed similar CD25, CD122, CD69, and CD44 but decreased CD127 (IL7Rα) compared to its WT control (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b showing expression of activation markers.

claim: Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre naïve OT2 T cells displayed similar CD25, CD69, CD122 and CD127 but noticeably decreased CD44 expression compared to their WT controls.
source: Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre naïve OT2 T cells displayed similar CD25, CD69, CD122 and CD127 but noticeably decreased CD44 expression compared to their WT controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1c showing expression of activation markers.

claim: CD45.1-CD45.2+Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre donor derived OT2 cells were noticeably low in percentages and numbers within the gated CD4+TCRVα2+ OT2 population in dLNs and spleen on day 7 after immunization.
source: On day 7 after immunization, CD45.1-CD45.2+Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre (Figure 6a,b) and Thy1.1-Thy1.2+ Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre (Figure 6f,g) donor derived OT2 cells were noticeably low in percentages and numbers within the gated CD4+TCRVα2+or CD4+TCRVβ2+ OT2 population in draining LNs (dLNs) and spleen.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 6a and 6b showing reduced donor OT2 cell numbers.

claim: Thy1.1-Thy1.2+ Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre donor derived OT2 cells were noticeably low in percentages and numbers within the gated CD4+TCRVβ2+ OT2 population in dLNs and spleen on day 7 after immunization.
source: On day 7 after immunization, CD45.1-CD45.2+Rptorf/f-Cd4Cre (Figure 6a,b) and Thy1.1-Thy1.2+ Rictorf/f-Cd4Cre (Figure 6f,g) donor derived OT2 cells were noticeably low in percentages and numbers within the gated CD4+TCRVα2+or CD4+TCRVβ2+ OT2 population in draining LNs (dLNs) and spleen.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 6f and 6g showing reduced donor OT2 cell numbers.

claim: Rptor-deficient donor OT2 T cells contained much lower percentages of CXCR5+PD1+ Tfh cells than did their WT controls.
source: Moreover, Rptor (Figure 6a bottom panel, 6c)- or Rictor (Figure 6f bottom panel, 6g)-deficient donor OT2 T cells contained much lower percentages of CXCR5+PD1+ Tfh cells than did their WT controls
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 6a and 6c showing reduced Tfh percentages.

claim: Rictor-deficient donor OT2 T cells contained much lower percentages of CXCR5+PD1+ Tfh cells than did their WT controls.
source: Moreover, Rptor (Figure 6a bottom panel, 6c)- or Rictor (Figure 6f bottom panel, 6g)-deficient donor OT2 T cells contained much lower percentages of CXCR5+PD1+ Tfh cells than did their WT controls
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 6f and 6h showing reduced Tfh percentages.

claim: Naïve CD4+ T cells intrinsically required both mTORC1 and mTORC2 to differentiate into Tfh cells.
source: Thus, data from adoptive transfer experiments demonstrated that naïve CD4+ T cells intrinsically required both mTORC1 and mTORC2 to differentiate into Tfh cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the adoptive transfer data in Figure 6.

claim: Rptor deficient OT2 T cells had similar percentages of dead cells compared with WT controls.
source: Rptor deficient OT2 T cells, including both Tfh and non-Tfh populations, had similar percentages of dead cells compared with WT controls (Figure 6e).
evidence: Demonstrated by Live/Dead staining data in Figure 6e showing similar death rates.

claim: Rictor deficient OT2 T cells showed increased death rates.
source: In contrast, Rictor deficient OT2 T cells showed increased death rates (Figure 6j).
evidence: Demonstrated by Live/Dead staining data in Figure 6j showing increased death rates.

claim: Rictor but not Raptor deficiency led to increased death of CD4+ T cells during immune responses.
source: Thus, Rictor but not Raptor deficiency led to increased death of CD4+ T cells during immune responses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the death rate data in Figure 6e and 6j.

claim: Raptor-deficient OT2 T cells displayed an obvious defect in proliferation 3, 5, and 7 days after immunization.
source: WT OT2 T cells demonstrated vigorous proliferation following immunization. In the absence of Raptor, OT2 T cells displayed an obvious defect in proliferation 3, 5, and 7 days after immunization (Figure 7a).
evidence: Demonstrated by CFSE dilution data in Figure 7a showing impaired proliferation.

claim: Proliferation of Raptor-deficient OT2 T cells was defective following in vitro TCR stimulation.
source: Similarly, proliferation of Raptor-deficient OT2 T cells was defective following in vitro TCR stimulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a)
evidence: Demonstrated by CFSE dilution data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1a showing impaired proliferation in vitro.

claim: Raptor-deficient OT2 T cells did not have severe defects in upregulation of T cell activation markers CD69 and CD44 with the exception of decreased CD25 upregulation.
source: Similarly, proliferation of Raptor-deficient OT2 T cells was defective following in vitro TCR stimulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a) without severe defects in upregulation of T cell activation markers CD69 and CD44 with the exception of decreased CD25 upregulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b)
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1b showing activation marker expression.

claim: CXCR5+ or PD1+ Tfh cells, differentiated from WT naïve CD4 T cells, began to appear after at least six divisions.
source: CXCR5+ or PD1+ Tfh cells, differentiated from WT naïve CD4 T cells, began to appear after at least six divisions (Figure 7b–e).
evidence: Demonstrated by CFSE dilution and Tfh marker staining data in Figure 7b-e showing Tfh appearance after division 6.

claim: Some Raptor-deficient OT2 cells eventually reached more than six divisions 7 days after immunization.
source: While delayed in proliferative expansion, some Raptor-deficient OT2 cells eventually reached more than six divisions 7 days after immunization.
evidence: This is observed from the CFSE dilution data in Figure 7a showing some cells reaching higher divisions.

claim: The PD1+/PD1- and CXCR5+/CXCR5- ratios in individual divisions were much lower for Raptor-deficient OT2 T cells than for WT controls.
source: However, the PD1+/PD1- and CXCR5+/CXCR5- ratios in individual divisions were much lower for Raptor-deficient OT2 T cells than for WT controls.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification data in Figure 7c and 7e showing reduced Tfh marker ratios per division.

claim: Raptor/mTORC1 not only promoted proliferation of CD4 T cells to reach the needed divisions after activation to become Tfh cells but also played an important role for expanded T cells to differentiate into Tfh cells.
source: Thus, Raptor/mTORC1 not only promoted proliferation of CD4 T cells to reach the needed divisions after activation to become Tfh cells but also played an important role for expanded T cells to differentiate into Tfh cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the proliferation and Tfh differentiation data in Figure 7a-e.

claim: Rictor-deficient OT2 T cells proliferated at similar rates compared with controls following in vitro TCR stimulation.
source: Unlike Raptor/mTORC1 deficiency, Rictor-deficient OT2 T cells proliferated and upregulated CD69 and CD25 at similar rates/levels compared with controls following in vitro TCR stimulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: Demonstrated by CFSE dilution data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1c showing similar proliferation.

claim: Rictor-deficient OT2 T cells upregulated CD69 and CD25 at similar levels compared with controls following in vitro TCR stimulation.
source: Unlike Raptor/mTORC1 deficiency, Rictor-deficient OT2 T cells proliferated and upregulated CD69 and CD25 at similar rates/levels compared with controls following in vitro TCR stimulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1d showing activation marker expression.

claim: CD44 levels could be upregulated in Rictor-deficient OT2 T cells, though they remained lower than stimulated WT controls.
source: CD44 levels could also be upregulated, though they remained lower than stimulated WT controls.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1d showing CD44 upregulation.

claim: Proliferation of adoptively transferred Rictor-deficient OT2 T cells was not obviously impaired compared to WT controls in recipient mice after immunization.
source: Furthermore, after immunization, proliferation of adoptively transferred Rictor-deficient OT2 T cells was not obviously impaired compared to WT controls in recipient mice (Figure 7f).
evidence: Demonstrated by CFSE dilution data in Figure 7f showing similar proliferation in vivo.

claim: CXCR5+/CXCR5- ratios in individual divisions after six divisions were decreased in Rictor-deficient OT2 T cells compared with WT controls.
source: However, their CXCR5+/CXCR5- ratios in individual divisions after six divisions were decreased compared with WT controls (Figure 7g,h).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification data in Figure 7h showing reduced CXCR5 ratios per division.

claim: The PD1+/PD1- ratios in Rictor-deficient OT2 T cells were not different from WT control in division 6.
source: The PD1+/PD1- ratios in Rictor-deficient OT2 T cells were not different from WT control in division 6 but displayed a tendency of decline after division 7, although the decreases were only statistically significant after division 10 (Figure 7i,j).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification data in Figure 7j showing PD1 ratios per division.

claim: The PD1+/PD1- ratios in Rictor-deficient OT2 T cells displayed a tendency of decline after division 7.
source: The PD1+/PD1- ratios in Rictor-deficient OT2 T cells were not different from WT control in division 6 but displayed a tendency of decline after division 7, although the decreases were only statistically significant after division 10 (Figure 7i,j).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification data in Figure 7j showing PD1 ratios per division.

claim: Tfh differentiation, rather than T cell activation and proliferation, selectively required Rictor/mTORC2.
source: Together, these observations suggested that Tfh differentiation, rather than T cell activation and proliferation, selectively required Rictor/mTORC2.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the proliferation and Tfh differentiation data in Figure 7f-j.

claim: The PI3K/Akt pathway plays an important role in Tfh differentiation.
source: Recent studies have revealed that the PI3K/Akt pathway plays an important role in Tfh differentiation (Gigoux et al., 2009; Stone et al., 2015; Rolf et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Akt phosphorylation at Ser473 decreased in Rictor/mTORC2-deficient T cells following TCR engagement.
source: Following TCR engagement, we observed apparently decreased Akt phosphorylation at Ser473, an mTORC2-dependent event, but not S6 phosphorylation, an mTORC1-dependent event, in Rictor/mTORC2-deficient T cells (Figure 8a, b).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot and flow cytometry data in Figure 8a and 8b showing decreased Akt S473 phosphorylation.

claim: S6 phosphorylation was not decreased in Rictor/mTORC2-deficient T cells following TCR engagement.
source: Following TCR engagement, we observed apparently decreased Akt phosphorylation at Ser473, an mTORC2-dependent event, but not S6 phosphorylation, an mTORC1-dependent event, in Rictor/mTORC2-deficient T cells (Figure 8a, b).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot and flow cytometry data in Figure 8a and 8b showing normal S6 phosphorylation.

claim: Akt phosphorylation at Ser473 is an mTORC2-dependent event.
source: Following TCR engagement, we observed apparently decreased Akt phosphorylation at Ser473, an mTORC2-dependent event, but not S6 phosphorylation, an mTORC1-dependent event, in Rictor/mTORC2-deficient T cells (Figure 8a, b).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mTORC2 function.

claim: S6 phosphorylation is an mTORC1-dependent event.
source: Following TCR engagement, we observed apparently decreased Akt phosphorylation at Ser473, an mTORC2-dependent event, but not S6 phosphorylation, an mTORC1-dependent event, in Rictor/mTORC2-deficient T cells (Figure 8a, b).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mTORC1 function.

claim: GSK-3β phosphorylation at Ser9 residue decreased in Rictor-deficient CD4 T cells.
source: Concordant with decreased Akt phosphorylation, GSK-3β phosphorylation at Ser9 residue, an Akt mediated event, also decreased in these cells (Figure 8a).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot data in Figure 8a showing decreased GSK-3β S9 phosphorylation.

claim: GSK-3β phosphorylation at Ser9 is an Akt mediated event.
source: Concordant with decreased Akt phosphorylation, GSK-3β phosphorylation at Ser9 residue, an Akt mediated event, also decreased in these cells (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Akt signaling.

claim: mTORC2 deficiency resulted in impaired Akt activation in CD4 T cells following TCR stimulation.
source: Thus, mTORC2 deficiency resulted in impaired Akt activation in CD4 T cells following TCR stimulation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the Akt phosphorylation data in Figure 8a and 8b.

claim: Expression of AktS473D increased PD1+CXCR5+ Tfh cells within Rictor-deficient OT2 T cells by two-fold.
source: Seven days after immunization, we observed a two-fold increase of PD1+CXCR5+ Tfh cells within GFP+TCRVα2+Vβ5+CD4+Rictor-deficient OT2 T cells expressing AktS473D compared with those expressing GFP alone (Figures 8c,d).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 8c and 8d showing increased Tfh differentiation with AktS473D expression.

claim: The effect of AktS473D on Tfh differentiation was correlated with its ability to upregulate Bcl-6 expression.
source: Such an effect of AktS473D on Tfh differentiation was correlated with its ability to upregulate Bcl-6 expression (Figure 8e)
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 8e showing increased Bcl-6 expression with AktS473D.

claim: AktS473D improved cell survival of Rictor-deficient OT2 T cells.
source: Such an effect of AktS473D on Tfh differentiation was correlated with its ability to upregulate Bcl-6 expression (Figure 8e) and to improve cell survival (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by Live/Dead staining data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 showing improved survival.

claim: Rictor-deficient OT2 T cells expressing AktS473D were still about 50% fewer Tfh cells than WT OT2 T cells.
source: Of note, Rictor-deficient OT2 T cells expressing AktS473D were still about 50% fewer Tfh cells than WT OT2 T cells (Figure 8c,d).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 8c and 8d showing partial rescue of Tfh differentiation.

claim: mTORC2 promoted Tfh differentiation via both Akt-dependent and -independent mechanisms.
source: Together, these observations suggested that mTORC2 promoted Tfh differentiation via both Akt-dependent and -independent mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that AktS473D only partially rescued Tfh differentiation in Rictor-deficient cells.

claim: The Wnt/β-catenin/TCF1 axis plays an important role in Tfh differentiation.
source: Recent studies reveal that the Wnt/β-catenin/TCF1 axis plays an important role in Tfh differentiation, at least by increasing Bcl-6 and ASCL2 expression (Choi et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: GSK3β negatively controls the Wnt/β-catenin/TCF1 axis by directly phosphorylating β-catenin to trigger its degradation.
source: Because GSK3β negatively controls the Wnt/β-catenin/TCF1 axis by directly phosphorylating β-catenin to trigger its degradation, and Akt phosphorylates and inactivates GSK3β (Staal et al., 2008; Hur and Zhou, 2010)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Akt phosphorylates and inactivates GSK3β.
source: Because GSK3β negatively controls the Wnt/β-catenin/TCF1 axis by directly phosphorylating β-catenin to trigger its degradation, and Akt phosphorylates and inactivates GSK3β (Staal et al., 2008; Hur and Zhou, 2010)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Rictor-deficient Tfh, naïve, and non-Tfh effector CD4 T cells expressed lower levels of β-catenin and TCF1 than did their WT controls.
source: As Figure 8f shows, Rictor-deficient Tfh, naïve, and non-Tfh effector CD4 T cells expressed lower levels of β-catenin and TCF1 than did their WT controls.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 8f showing reduced β-catenin and TCF1 expression.

claim: Both mRNA levels of TCF1 (Tcf7) and β-catenin responsive genes ASCL2 and c-Myc decreased in Rictor-deficient Tfh cells.
source: Additionally, both mRNA levels of TCF1 (Tcf7) and β-catenin responsive genes ASCL2 and c-Myc also decreased in Rictor-deficient Tfh cells (Figure 8g)
evidence: Demonstrated by RT-PCR data in Figure 8g showing reduced mRNA levels.

claim: mTORC2 deficiency diminished β-catenin and TCF1 expression in CD4 T cells.
source: Additionally, both mRNA levels of TCF1 (Tcf7) and β-catenin responsive genes ASCL2 and c-Myc also decreased in Rictor-deficient Tfh cells (Figure 8g), indicating that mTORC2 deficiency diminished β-catenin and TCF1 expression in CD4 T cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the β-catenin and TCF1 expression data in Figure 8f and 8g.

claim: Expression of AktS473D increased TCF1 expression.
source: Importantly, expression of AktS473D increased TCF1 expression (Figure 8h)
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 8h showing increased TCF1 with AktS473D expression.

claim: Overexpression of the TCF1-p45 long isoform increased Tfh differentiation about two-fold.
source: Importantly, expression of AktS473D increased TCF1 expression (Figure 8h) and overexpression of the TCF1-p45 long isoform capable of binding β-catenin, but not the TCF1-p33 short isoform lacking β-catenin-interacting domain, increased Tfh differentiation about two-fold (Figure 8c,d) .
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 8c and 8d showing increased Tfh differentiation with TCF1-p45 expression.

claim: The TCF1-p33 short isoform lacking β-catenin-interacting domain did not increase Tfh differentiation.
source: Importantly, expression of AktS473D increased TCF1 expression (Figure 8h) and overexpression of the TCF1-p45 long isoform capable of binding β-catenin, but not the TCF1-p33 short isoform lacking β-catenin-interacting domain, increased Tfh differentiation about two-fold (Figure 8c,d) .
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 8c and 8d showing no rescue with TCF1-p33 expression.

claim: TCF1 has intrinsic HDAC activity embedded within a 30 amino acid (Q192-L221) region.
source: TCF1 has recently demonstrated intrinsic HDAC activity embedded within a 30 amino acid (Q192-L221) region (Xing et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Xing et al., 2016.

claim: Forced expression of a TCF1-Loop34 mutant, which lacks the HDAC domain, failed to show a 'rescue' effect.
source: Forced expression of a TCF1-Loop34 mutant, which lacks the HDAC domain, failed to show a 'rescue' effect, suggesting a contribution from the TCF1 HDAC activity for Tfh differentiation (Figure 8c,d).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 8c and 8d showing no rescue with TCF1-Loop34 expression.

claim: TCF1 HDAC activity contributes to Tfh differentiation.
source: Forced expression of a TCF1-Loop34 mutant, which lacks the HDAC domain, failed to show a 'rescue' effect, suggesting a contribution from the TCF1 HDAC activity for Tfh differentiation (Figure 8c,d).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the HDAC-deficient TCF1 mutant failed to rescue Tfh differentiation.

claim: TCF1-p45 was able to upregulate Bcl-6 expression in Rictor deficient OT2 T cells.
source: Correlated with their ability to rescue Tfh differentiation, TCF1-p45 was able to upregulate Bcl-6 expression in Rictor deficient OT2 T cells (Figure 8i).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 8i showing increased Bcl-6 with TCF1-p45 expression.

claim: Decreased TCF1 expression may at least partly contribute to the failure of Rictor/mTORC2-deficient CD4 T cells to differentiate to Tfh cells.
source: Together, these observations suggest that decreased TCF1 expression may at least partly contribute to the failure of Rictor/mTORC2-deficient CD4 T cells to differentiate to Tfh cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the TCF1 rescue experiments in Figure 8.

claim: A recent study showed that inhibition of mTORC1 with rapamycin or reduction of mTOR expression with shRNA promotes Tfh differentiation following lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus infection.
source: A recent study showed that inhibition of mTORC1 with rapamycin or reduction of mTOR expression with shRNA promotes Tfh differentiation following lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus infection, concluding that mTORC1 negatively controls Tfh differentiation (Ray et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a citation to a previous study by Ray et al., 2015.

claim: Another study has found that a hypomorphic mutation of mTOR reduces Tfh and GC responses in mice immunized with sheep red blood cells.
source: However, another study has found that a hypomorphic mutation of mTOR reduces Tfh and GC responses in mice immunized with sheep red blood cells, concluding that mTOR promoted Tfh differentiation (Ramiscal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a citation to a previous study by Ramiscal et al., 2015.

claim: Rapamycin has been found to inhibit GC formation and Ig class-switch in B cells upon influenza infection.
source: Additionally, rapamycin has also been found to inhibit GC formation and Ig class-switch in B cells upon influenza infection, although whether rapamycin directly acts on T cells, B cells, or both is unclear (Keating et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a citation to a previous study by Keating et al., 2013.

claim: mTOR is a serine/threonine kinase that can integrate multiple signals to control cell growth, proliferation, differentiation, metabolism, and survival.
source: The mammalian/mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) is a serine/threonine kinase that can integrate multiple signals to control cell growth, proliferation, differentiation, metabolism, and survival (Laplante and Sabatini, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mTOR function supported by citation.

claim: mTOR signals mainly through two distinct complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2.
source: mTOR signals mainly through two distinct complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2, which are defined, respectively, by the signature components regulatory-associated protein of mTOR (Raptor) and rapamycin-insensitive companion of mTOR (Rictor).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mTOR complexes.

claim: mTORC1 is defined by the signature component Raptor.
source: mTOR signals mainly through two distinct complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2, which are defined, respectively, by the signature components regulatory-associated protein of mTOR (Raptor) and rapamycin-insensitive companion of mTOR (Rictor).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mTORC1 composition.

claim: mTORC2 is defined by the signature component Rictor.
source: mTOR signals mainly through two distinct complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2, which are defined, respectively, by the signature components regulatory-associated protein of mTOR (Raptor) and rapamycin-insensitive companion of mTOR (Rictor).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mTORC2 composition.

claim: mTORC1 phosphorylates S6K and 4EBP1 to promote ribosome biogenesis, cap-dependent translation, and lipid and nucleic acid synthesis.
source: mTORC1 phosphorylates multiple substrates such as ribosomal protein S6 kinase (S6K) and eIF4E-binding protein 1 (4EBP1) to promote ribosome biogenesis, cap-dependent translation, and lipid and nucleic acid synthesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mTORC1 function.

claim: mTORC2 phosphorylates PKCα, SGK1, and Akt at serine 473 residue to regulate cytoskeleton reorganization, metabolism, and survival.
source: mTORC2 phosphorylates completely different effector molecules such as PKCα, glucocorticoid-induced protein kinase 1 (SGK1), and Akt at serine 473 residue to regulate cytoskeleton reorganization, metabolism, and survival.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mTORC2 function.

claim: The PI3K/Akt, RasGRP1/Ras/Erk, and PKCθ-CARMA1 pathways are critical for TCR-induced mTORC1 and mTORC2 activation in T cells.
source: In T cells, the PI3K/Akt, RasGRP1/Ras/Erk, and PKCθ-CARMA1 pathways are critical for TCR-induced mTORC1 and mTORC2 activation (Gorentla et al., 2011; Hamilton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: mTOR and its tight regulation are pivotal for proper T cell activation.
source: mTOR and its tight regulation are pivotal for proper T cell activation (Chi, 2012; O'Brien et al., 2012; O'Brien et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2011)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: mTOR is important for Th1/2/17 differentiation.
source: mTOR and its tight regulation are pivotal for proper T cell activation (Chi, 2012; O'Brien et al., 2012; O'Brien et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2011), Th1/2/17 differentiation (Delgoffe et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2012)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: mTOR is important for effector/memory CD8 T cell differentiation.
source: mTOR and its tight regulation are pivotal for proper T cell activation (Chi, 2012; O'Brien et al., 2012; O'Brien et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2011), Th1/2/17 differentiation (Delgoffe et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2012), effector/memory CD8 T cell differentiation (Araki et al., 2009; Rao et al., 2010)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: mTOR is important for Treg function.
source: mTOR and its tight regulation are pivotal for proper T cell activation (Chi, 2012; O'Brien et al., 2012; O'Brien et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2011), Th1/2/17 differentiation (Delgoffe et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2012), effector/memory CD8 T cell differentiation (Araki et al., 2009; Rao et al., 2010), Treg function (Park et al., 2013; Zeng et al., 2013)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: mTOR is important for iNKT maturation and effector lineage differentiation.
source: mTOR and its tight regulation are pivotal for proper T cell activation (Chi, 2012; O'Brien et al., 2012; O'Brien et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2011), Th1/2/17 differentiation (Delgoffe et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2012), effector/memory CD8 T cell differentiation (Araki et al., 2009; Rao et al., 2010), Treg function (Park et al., 2013; Zeng et al., 2013), and iNKT maturation and effector lineage differentiation (Wu et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2014; Shin et al., 2014; Wei et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2015; Prevot et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2014)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: mTOR is important for extrinsic control of intrathymic αβ T and γδ T cell development.
source: mTOR and its tight regulation are pivotal for proper T cell activation (Chi, 2012; O'Brien et al., 2012; O'Brien et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2011), Th1/2/17 differentiation (Delgoffe et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2012), effector/memory CD8 T cell differentiation (Araki et al., 2009; Rao et al., 2010), Treg function (Park et al., 2013; Zeng et al., 2013), and iNKT maturation and effector lineage differentiation (Wu et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2014; Shin et al., 2014; Wei et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2015; Prevot et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2014), and extrinsic control of intrathymic αβ T and γδ T cell development (Wang et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.
